title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI and deepfake technology were used to fabricate a news article. The article falsely placed two real, named public figures in an interview that never happened, and used that fabricated content to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure did not occur inside a legitimate AI deployment, but rather in the deliberate misuse of generative AI tools to produce convincing false media for fraudulent purposes.

The scam operated at the content-creation stage, before any victim encountered a financial product. Catching it would have required either platform-level detection of synthetically generated impersonation content or audience verification of the named figures and the claimed event, neither of which happened automatically. ASIC's reported figures show this is not an isolated case but a pattern, with the regulator removing tens of thousands of such scams and recording sharp percentage increases across phishing and fake investment platform categories.

What is not established is the identity of the individuals or groups responsible for creating the fake article, how many people were harmed by it, or whether any funds were lost to the Boulder Sparhaven platform specifically. The ASIC figures are from a regulator's own research release and represent reported and detected cases, not a verified total of all scam activity.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven never actually occurred. This fabricated story exemplifies a growing type of scam that uses artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to create convincing but false investment opportunities. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent online.

ASIC's new research reveals alarming growth in investment scams, with the regulator taking down 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms surged 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated public figures. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, and websites before requesting personal details. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and to distrust opportunities that seem too good to be true.
